opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we're at a really exciting inflection point. For a long time, machine learning was mostly about perception: images, speech, text. Science is different because we actually know a lot about how the world works. We have the Schrödinger equation, we have the laws of thermodynamics, we have symmetries. So the question becomes: how do you combine that deep prior knowledge with the flexibility of learned models?

I see a few layers to this. The first is acceleration of simulation. A lot of scientific computing, things like density functional theory or molecular dynamics, is extremely expensive. If you can train neural networks to emulate those simulators, and especially if you build in the right symmetries, like equivariance to rotations and translations, you can get orders of magnitude speedups while staying physically faithful. That alone changes what's feasible.

The second layer is generative design. Instead of only predicting the properties of a molecule or material you already have, you ask the model to propose candidates with the properties you want. That inverts the traditional pipeline, and it's where diffusion models and related techniques have been surprisingly powerful.

The third layer, which I find the most interesting, is closing the loop with experiments. Models propose, simulations filter, a lab or an automated platform tests, and the data flows back in. That's essentially active learning or Bayesian experimental design at the scale of a whole research program. It starts to look like an AI-assisted version of the scientific method itself.

And then of course there are the large language models, which are becoming quite good at reading literature, writing code, and orchestrating these tools. I don't think they replace the physics-based models, but they can act as the glue: an agent that knows which simulator to call, how to set up the experiment, and how to interpret the result.

The reason I care so much about this is the problems at stake. Think about materials for carbon capture, better batteries, new catalysts, new medicines. These are search problems over astronomically large spaces, and they matter enormously for climate and health. If AI can make that search even ten times more efficient, that's a big deal for the world. So for me, AI for science is one of the most meaningful places to apply this technology, maybe more meaningful than yet another chatbot.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is actually the most exciting thing happening in AI right now, more exciting to me than chatbots, honestly.

The way I see it, science has always been a loop: you observe, you build a model, you make predictions, you run an experiment, and you update. For a few hundred years the bottleneck has been the human in that loop. We can only hold so much in our heads, we can only read so many papers, we can only run so many experiments. What's changing is that AI is starting to attack every single stage of that loop at once.

Take simulation. A huge fraction of science is just solving equations we already know: Schrödinger's equation for molecules, Navier-Stokes for fluids, Maxwell's equations for materials. We know the physics, we just can't afford to compute it. Density functional theory on a molecule of a few hundred atoms is already painful, and molecular dynamics at the accuracy you actually want is hopeless at the scales that matter. So the first big win is learned surrogates. You train a neural network on expensive simulations and then it runs a thousand or a million times faster. Weather forecasting is the cleanest example. A few years ago people laughed at the idea, and now the learned models are beating the big numerical weather centers at a fraction of the compute. That same story is playing out in materials, in drug discovery, in catalysis.

The thing I'd stress, and this is where a lot of my own work has been, is that you can't just throw a vanilla transformer at these problems. Nature has structure: symmetries, conservation laws, the fact that physics doesn't care how you rotate your coordinate system. If you build that into the architecture, with equivariant networks and so on, you need far less data and you generalize much better. Data in science is expensive. You don't have the internet to scrape; you have a few thousand DFT calculations. So inductive bias really matters here, in a way that it maybe matters less in language.

The second stage is generative design. Once you have a fast, accurate model of how a molecule or material behaves, you can flip it around and ask: give me a molecule with these properties. That's where diffusion models and the like come in. And then you close the loop with automated labs, where a robot actually synthesizes the candidate, measures it, and feeds the result back. That's the self-driving lab idea, and I think it's going to be enormous.

Now, the hype question. People ask whether AI is going to "do science" on its own. I'm more measured there. Right now these tools are superb at interpolation inside the regime they've seen, and much shakier at genuine extrapolation, which is where discovery actually lives. And there's a trust issue. A learned surrogate that's wrong is wrong silently, whereas a physics solver at least fails in a way you understand. So uncertainty quantification, knowing when the model doesn't know, is not a nice-to-have, it's central. That's partly why I keep coming back to Bayesian ideas even in this very deep-learning world.

But even with those caveats, the trajectory is clear. If you can make simulation a thousand times cheaper, you change what questions are even worth asking. That's not an incremental improvement, that's a different kind of science. And climate, energy, new materials for batteries, new antibiotics, these are the problems that actually matter for the planet. So if I had to tell a young researcher where to go, I'd say: don't just build another chatbot. Go sit next to a chemist.

astra-6.text:
I think this is one of the most exciting applications of AI. Science often involves an inverse problem: you observe something, and you want to understand the underlying system that produced it. Machine learning gives us powerful tools for doing that, particularly when the observations are complex or the space of possible explanations is very large.

But the interesting opportunity is to combine learning with what we already know about the world. In physics, for example, we have symmetries and conservation laws. If you build those into a model, it doesn’t have to rediscover everything from data. That can make learning much more efficient and help the model generalize.

You can also move from predicting properties to proposing things: a molecule, a material, or an experiment. Then you have a loop where the model proposes something, you test it, and the result improves the model. That could really accelerate discovery.

The crucial question is whether those proposals survive experimental testing. A model can give you a very plausible answer and still be wrong. So I see AI as becoming part of the scientific process, with experiments and uncertainty playing a central role.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an enormous opportunity. A lot of science involves an expensive cycle: you propose a hypothesis, run an experiment or a simulation, look at the result, and then decide what to try next. Machine learning can help at each of those steps, but perhaps the most interesting possibility is to connect them into a much faster loop.

Take discovering new materials. You might want a material with certain properties, but the space of possible structures is enormous. You can learn a model that predicts those properties, use it to propose promising candidates, and then test them with a more accurate simulation or in the laboratory. Those results become new training data.

But I think you have to be careful about what the model actually knows. If you’re searching for something genuinely new, you’re often moving outside the distribution of your training data. So uncertainty becomes very important: when should you trust the prediction, and when should you do another experiment?

And we should use the structure that science already gives us—symmetries, conservation laws, physical constraints. You don’t want to relearn all of physics from scratch if you can build some of that knowledge into the model. For me, the exciting direction is that combination: learning from data, respecting the underlying physics, and using experiments to continually correct the model.
